author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Measure shader-cache warm-up across cold and repeat PS2 launches
summary: Use a deterministic effect route across first visit, immediate replay, app restart, and optional system restart to learn which hitches disappear after pipeline compilation and whether the cache persists normally.
heroAlt: Vulkan 1.3 graphic representing graphics-pipeline and shader-cache behavior

blocks.text: Map first-encounter effects across lifecycle boundaries

A shader or pipeline cache should reduce some first-encounter compilation work after materials and effects have been seen. To test it, use a route with named effect landmarks and preserve the cache between passes. Compare a first visit, immediate replay, ordinary app restart, and only then an optional Android restart. Do not clear application data unless cache-rebuild behavior is the explicit separate experiment.
Clearing cache between every pass makes all launches cold and prevents persistence measurement. Back up configuration before any deliberate data-clear test.
Prepare a landmark and lifecycle table

items: A normal save before a deterministic route containing several distinct effects.
One renderer and system driver held constant throughout the sequence.
A frame-time overlay or synchronized recording with stable overhead.
The initial cache state documented before the first visit.
Enough storage space and no cleanup utility scheduled during testing.

blocks.text: Run first visit, replay, app restart, and system restart

items: 1. Document the cache state and cold-boot the route without deleting files.
2. Mark every hitch by timestamp and visible effect landmark.
3. Return to the same save and replay immediately with no settings changes.
4. Close the emulator normally, reopen it, and run a third pass.
5. Compare which hitches disappear, shrink, or recur at identical landmarks.
6. Restart Android and repeat only if system-lifecycle persistence matters.
7. Inspect logs and cache timestamps without modifying their contents.
8. Store the four-pass table before testing any deliberate cache deletion.

blocks.text: Immediate replay tests in-session reuse; app restart tests whether compiled data survives a normal process lifecycle; system restart tests persistence across a broader boundary. A hitch that repeats at every identical doorway may instead be storage or synchronization work, while irregular late-session hitches may be thermal or background activity.
The classification must follow repeatable landmark behavior across the defined lifecycle stages.

items: First-visit hitches are mapped to named effects or locations.
Immediate replay uses the same route and unchanged profile.
App restart occurs without cache deletion.
System restart is tested separately and only when needed.
Logs or timestamps support the persistence conclusion.

blocks.text: Sequences to restart from the beginning

items: Android or a cleaner removes cache mid-sequence: disable the cleanup and repeat.
A driver or renderer changes between passes: begin a new table.
Random encounters alter effects: choose a deterministic save.
The second pass begins hotter: normalize thermal state.

blocks.text: Preserve the proven cache and normal lifecycle

Disable diagnostic overlays, keep the valid cache, restore normal background-cleanup policy, and cold-boot the title once. If a deliberate deletion was tested later, allow one complete warm-up route before judging everyday performance again.
One-time work is not automatically shader compilation

Texture uploads, decompression, disc reads, and game initialization can also disappear on replay. Use renderer logs and effect correlation to support a shader label, and keep uncertain hitches classified as first-visit events rather than overstating the cause.
